Although it was not difficult to predict that the course of events was leading to this. And we live for today. If an individual person can live for today like that, the state should not live like that.

Inal Khashig: The state somehow manages to.

Astamur Tania: It should still plan its future, the society.

Inal Khashig: I would like to switch to another topic now. Periodically, we are reminded of the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, which continuously remains at a dead end. Last time, we discussed how Georgian perceptions of Abkhazia and the Abkhaz people have changed, particularly through the influence of Pavel Ingorokva’s theory, which took a strong hold in Georgian thought.

Shortly after our conversation, I watched an interview with the Georgian historian Tsurtsumia on a Georgian YouTube channel. He noted that Ingorokva’s theory is actually marginal and lacks official state support.

Nevertheless, just the day before yesterday, I came across a vividly animated video. It was set in Sukhumi on the embankment, depicting peaceful civilians in a setting reminiscent of 1992, when a Russian military aircraft suddenly swoops in and begins bombing. The people are shown fleeing the embankment, trying to escape by ship or heading into the mountains.

Astamur Tania: Those are slightly different scenes, probably. Maybe it is one pie, but different slices.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but you see, this is proceeding very actively – why I understood this is not only Ingorokva’s theory about who the Abkhaz are and what their origin is, but in Georgian society the understanding of what the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict was is changing very actively. And what happened 33 years ago, 34 years ago. How the war started.

According to this cartoon… A cartoon is a certain part of upbringing. It also has its own audience. Directed at a certain audience. At children. It is important for me to understand why the Georgians converted this conflict into a conflict not between Georgians and Abkhaz, but a certain conflict between Russia and Georgia.

Astamur Tania: That is completely understandable, as acknowledging it would require admitting responsibility for starting the armed conflict. By the way, Shevardnadze did admit this responsibility—and while he claimed Kitovani was to blame, Kitovani was not the Defense Minister of Russia, but of Georgia. Everyone remembers, and archival footage still shows, how this war began and how the local Georgian population reacted.

Acknowledging this would require erasing entire sections of history. Instead, there is an effort to reshape the narrative of 1992 and merge it with the events of 2008, framing everything around legislation and the narrative of post-2008 occupation. Yet, a detailed examination—including the report by the International Fact-Finding Commission led by Heidi Tagliavini—confirmed that responsibility for initiating military action in both instances lay with the Georgian side.

Naturally, there is a desire to obscure this in the media space to advance narratives about occupation, aiming to shape international opinion to justify a forceful resolution or delegitimize the Abkhazian state.

We must react to this. The fact that animated videos are being produced on this topic shows an intent to pass this worldview down to the next generation. If we carry such a perspective into the future, achieving a peaceful settlement or joint progress will be extremely difficult. This is why it is essential to present the fullest possible picture, starting with the factual timeline.

Regarding Zura Tsurtsumia’s comments: first, it is positive that Georgian-Abkhaz relations are being examined at a solid academic level, attempting to move beyond today’s propaganda clichés toward a historical assessment of the conflict’s roots.

However, claiming that Ingorokva’s theory is marginal ignores reality in the Georgian media landscape, where it remains the most widespread view on the origins of the Abkhazian people. While prominent Georgian scholars considered it pseudoscientific—such as Javakhishvili, who noted that ancient Adyghe tribes inhabited Western Georgia prior to the Kartvelians and recognized the Apsilals and Abasgs as direct ancestors of modern Abkhaz—these classical works are largely ignored by mainstream media.

Instead, hate speech dominates the discourse among commentators—and we must acknowledge that hate speech exists on the Abkhaz side as well. Neither side benefits from this.

Objectively, neither we nor Georgia have any interest in a renewed armed conflict, which would yield disastrous consequences for both. Some in Georgian society may assume their larger population makes it an easy victory, but that is far from reality. We cannot afford to trigger such a dangerous cycle.

Both sides are equally served by abandoning hate speech and language that demeans human dignity and belittles culture, especially given that all human cultures, including Abkhazian and Georgian, are products of historical interaction and symbiosis.

Finally, addressing Tsurtsumia’s assertion—which is not unique to him—that the Abkhaz nation was deliberately engineered by Soviet authorities to counter Georgia: while Soviet policies influenced the development of both the Georgian and Abkhazian nations in the late 19th and 20th centuries, it is vital to recognize that the Abkhaz national identity was not an artificial creation.

In fact, during the 1930s and 1940s, deliberate repressive measures were used in an effort to suppress the formation of the Abkhaz nation.

Inal Khashig: That was when schools were closed.

Astamur Tania: Schools were closed, and the destruction of the intelligentsia—the bearers of this very idea—took place at that time. This inflicted a serious trauma.

But one must understand that this process is accomplished. It is an accomplished fact. And in dialogue with the Abkhaz, everyone must proceed from the premise that this is not simply an ethnos, but a formed nation. With its own ideas about borders, policy, with its own national mythology. This is not always equal to history. Here there is a completely different approach.

As I once spoke with an Abkhaz, he said in his heart: why did Gurandukht, the daughter of the Abkhaz king, marry Gurgen, the ruler of Tao-Klarjeti? Since then, the unification of the Abkhaz state with the Georgian one began. That is the feudal era. It is an accomplished fact. We can only look at it like that. It sounds like a parody.

The same applies to this issue. It is closer to us. These are already accomplished facts. We must take them into account. Proceed from the fact that this is a given. Second, there were in fact certain inaccuracies there.

I do not want to delve into that now. In itself, this attempt to approach the understanding of the origins of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict with a cool head, using academic material—if this happens more or less regularly, in the same calm atmosphere, then it seems to me that both societies can win from this.

Inal Khashig: On the other hand, it seems to me, given that this seems to be a recent event—the war is relatively a historical event, only 30 years ago—nevertheless, judging by what I read in social networks, certain articles, certain speeches of politicians or experts…

Astamur Tania: Very much so.

Inal Khashig: I still see a lot of statements specifically adjusting to the political opportunism of the moment. If you remember, in the 80s, in the 90s after the war, what were we called? Abkhaz separatists. Now you practically do not hear this term.

Astamur Tania: By the way, they started calling us Abkhaz separatists back during the war, and before that—Gudauta separatists. Although during that period Abkhazia had not yet declared that it was ceasing any relations with Georgia and was not going to live with it within common borders.

In its time, on the initiative of Georgian figures, the process of all kinds of division began in Abkhazia. They separated the Georgian sector from the Abkhaz State University. Then they withdrew the football team. Then they withdrew the Georgian faction from the Supreme Council. They began to sit separately. That is, they apparently assumed that gradually they would somehow paralyze things. And here the question arises: who was the separatist?

And the same with this term. And, by the way, “Gudauta separatists”—later this very term migrated into the documents of the United Nations. And for some time after the end of the war, when our authorities were already located in Sukhumi, they continued to call us Gudauta separatists. I think for the Abzhua Abkhaz this is a bit offensive. Gudauta-Abzzua separatists would have been sound better.

Inal Khashig: But, nevertheless, this term somehow went out of circulation. And we have already been switched to the idea that Abkhazia is a territory occupied by Russia. And at the same time, as for the Abkhaz—let us leave aside those social networks where we generally came down from the mountains, according to the Georgian version—in official rhetoric nothing is said about us anymore.

Astamur Tania: “Came down from the mountains” is also quite amusing, because on most of the coast, based on climatic conditions and the unhealthiness of this climate, it was practically impossible to live permanently. Even if you open the press of, say, the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it is evident that the affluent portion of the residents of the city of Sukhumi left Sukhumi for the summer period. Precisely when there was the peak of this disease, people left for the foothills, because living here was a bit dangerous.

Inal Khashig: And the most prosperous ones lived there.

Astamur Tania: Generally, we have a perception as if in the Middle Ages communications in Abkhazia—this applies to everything, we are talking about Abkhazia—ran along the coast like that; there was the Ancient Roman railway running, next to it the Byzantine highway, but in reality all communications passed through the foothills and across the ridges. It was later, with the arrival of the Russian Empire, that this network of communications familiar to us began to develop. And psychologically we begin to tie our perception of the past to what had already taken shape in the 19th and 20th centuries. There was no railway at the beginning of the 20th century yet.

Inal Khashig: This highway that exists now.

Astamur Tania: For example, construction of the Black Sea railway continued in 1918 still. The Russian Empire no longer existed, but it was unclear what would happen. But they continued to build it in the Gagra region in 1918. And now it seems that it was always there.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, I tried to understand. Why do they depict Abkhaz who did not participate in this conflict, or played some secondary role in this Georgian-Abkhaz conflict? In the war that took place in 1992-1993.

Astamur Tania: A moment is omitted. What quantity of weapons was transferred to Georgia under the Tashkent Agreement on the eve of the conflict? The Russian authorities of that time were far from being, to put it mildly, pro-Abkhaz.

This is evident from everything. This is visible if one reads at least the transcript of September 3 of the meeting of Shevardnadze, Yeltsin, Ardzinba, representatives of the North Caucasus, representatives of our various parliamentary deputations. Not only should documents be studied, one should read the transcript.

But why did Georgia start armed conflicts? It received at its disposal several motor rifle and tank divisions of the Transcaucasus Military District. Therefore, in their joy, they thought that it would be possible to quickly finish this business.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, why am I saying all this—I read an interesting Georgian perspective on why this is happening, that Abkhaz are being excluded from this conflict, that through such an exclusion—and, say, when a certain image of the enemy is removed from the Abkhaz in this conflict, in this war, if the Abkhaz played a non-primary role, it means they are not enemies. There is a hypothetical possibility they retain that later at some point we will make peace with them.

Astamur Tania: That is very hypothetical. In my opinion, it is impossible to do that. Because how can one take a segment of a section of thinking and take something out of there… It seems to me this is very much a laboratory theory.

Inal Khashig: But this is laboratory on the one hand, and on the other hand the Abkhaz themselves have their own perception of the war.

Astamur Tania: To reiterate: those in Georgia who deal with the Georgian-Abkhaz settlement or seek to study this issue must start from the accomplished fact of the Abkhazian nation’s existence. A nation cannot be treated as a third-party observer—it is an active subject. We are an active subject in our relations with Georgia. Recognized or unrecognized, by our internal structure, we are a nation—with our own statehood and our own distinct perception of both the past and the future.

Our perspectives may not always align, but if we look at history honestly, our centuries-long—even thousand-year-old—relations with various Kartvelian peoples, primarily Megrelians, cannot simply be painted in black-and-white. History saw different periods, including feudal wars, which, it should be noted, occurred internally among those groups as well. There was continuous interaction, symbiosis, and movement back and forth. This is why we find Megrelian surnames in Abkhazia, Abkhaz surnames in Zugdidi, and why Gali in particular serves as a concentrated microcosm where everything is intertwined.

We, too, must draw important policy conclusions from this. But there must be a foundational understanding that if there is a real desire to settle our relations or develop a pragmatic approach—though I do not expect major breakthroughs given our disagreements—it starts with recognizing that a political nation has formed here. Its members are not solely ethnic Abkhazians, but all citizens of Abkhazia. We, too, must recognize this and move away from a narrow communal mindset.

Inal Khashig: But, by the way, it is present.

Astamur Tania: That is natural, because that is where it started. But we must nevertheless move in the direction of a civic nation.

Inal Khashig: Well yes, a political nation. This distinction is crucial because, unfortunately, many people’s perception of the Abkhazian situation and where we stand today was shaped back in Soviet times.

Astamur Tania: In fact, the post-Stalin Soviet period wasn’t all bad. Despite setbacks during that recovery process, it was unthinkable to express such vile ideas in writing back then.

Inal Khashig: My point is slightly different. In Soviet times, the Abkhaz struggle focused on ethnic rights—opening schools, theaters, literary journals, and universities—since few anticipated the collapse of the Soviet Union. The political nation back then was subsumed under the concept of the ‘Soviet people,’ right?

Astamur Tania: Well, ‘the Soviet people’ was an ideological construct, though autonomous frameworks did exist.

Inal Khashig: Yet today, some still take a fragmented approach, viewing society purely as separate ethnic groups—Abkhaz, Armenians, Russians, and so on—rather than…

Astamur Tania: You mean moving toward a unified civic nation?

Inal Khashig: Exactly. That is essential.

Astamur Tania: That requires active political education. Some processes occur naturally: living within the same state fosters shared views on security, peaceful development, and the necessity of an independent Abkhazia. However, we must establish clear criteria for this political nation to avoid repeating the mistakes made in Georgia during the Gamsakhurdia era. As a polyethnic society, we must embed protections that guarantee the survival of the Abkhaz people. Our fellow citizens understand this foundational principle.

That brings us back to language. Over time, our entire society must achieve sufficient command of the Abkhaz language for daily communication. Naturally, our society will remain bilingual due to demographic and geopolitical realities. This is why Russian is constitutionally designated alongside Abkhaz. But ‘alongside’ must not mean replacing Abkhaz. Striking this balance requires preserving the Abkhaz language while maintaining interethnic harmony. We should engage Abkhaz academic circles and draw on international experience—such as the major initiatives used to revive and preserve Welsh alongside English.

Ultimately, we need a sense of proportion in both domestic and foreign policy. Though emotions run high, avoiding extremes is vital. A population of our size can only survive through moderation and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Having come full circle, it seems clear that the survival and development of Abkhazia depend on building an inclusive civic nation that encompasses all ethnic groups residing here as citizens…

Astamur Tania: Including Georgians, of course.

Inal Khashig: …who would also command the state language.

Astamur Tania: Regarding the Gali district specifically, we must rethink our policy. We must acknowledge that regardless of how they identify ethnically, the residents there represent a native Megrelian-Georgian population, many with historical Abkhaz roots.

Inal Khashig: We can dedicate a separate conversation to that topic. But building a civic nation—governed by the rule of law and grounded in our constitutional language framework—is key to securing our future so that we aren’t constantly fearing our own disappearance.

Astamur Tania: Though I think we are destined to sound the alarm for many years to come!

Inal Khashig: Building a civic nation takes time and represents a broader movement toward a state governed by the rule of law.

Astamur Tania: To end on a reassuring note: perhaps artificial intelligence will solve all these problems for us!

Inal Khashig: I hope so! On that note, we will wrap up today’s broadcast. Today, Astamur Tania and I discussed the Abkhaz language, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, and why these complex questions persist. Goodbye. Until new meetings. Thank you.

Astamur Tania: Thank you.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, people leave” – from a march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video blog
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Lawyer for rapist Ralph Carr urges court to halt case
World.content:
Prosecutors have called on a County Court judge not to delay sentencing rapist celebrity agent Ralph Carr after his defence team made a rare legal move to halt the case.

Last month, a jury found Carr guilty of raping a woman at his West Melbourne home three years ago, an allegation he denied. A longstanding suppression order was also lifted, identifying Carr.

The complainant was the key witness in the case, and gave evidence in front of the jury for at least five days.

Today, defence barrister Dermot Dann KC argued that the judge, Frank Gucciardo, should postpone plans to sentence Carr next week.

The move, known as a "stay", would open the door for Carr to apply for bail ahead of a legal challenge in the Court of Appeal.

Dermot Dann (front) told the court the guilty verdicts against Ralph Carr (left) were a miscarriage of justice. (ABC News)

Mr Dann said it was the first time in 35 years he had made such an application, and described the jury verdict as "the most obvious miscarriage of justice I've ever seen".

"Anyone who was in court who saw and heard the complainant give evidence in this trial should be very, very concerned; very, very uncomfortable about the guilty verdicts," he said.

" Anyone who does feel comfortable with verdicts has lost sight of what justice is and what justice means. "

However, prosecutor Matthew Fisher accused Mr Dann of making a "political and emotional" speech that was inappropriate and questioned whether it was designed to attract media attention.

Mr Fisher said the jury was aware of "issues" with some aspects of the complainant's evidence, but still decided beyond reasonable doubt that she was raped by Carr.

"Your honour should not entertain the stay application," he said.

In calling for a stay of sentence, Mr Dann referenced the cases of Robert Tait and Ronald Ryan, two men sentenced to hanging in Victoria in the 60s.

Tait's death sentence was eventually stayed, but Ryan's was not, making him the final man to be hanged in Australia.

Ronald Ryan is seen here between two police officers during his murder trial for murder. (ABC Archives)

Judge Gucciardo told Mr Dann his client was not the first person found guilty to proclaim their innocence and said it was not his task to re-assess the evidence considered by the jury.

"What we had was a very conscientious jury who listened to the evidence, who listened to your very complete and, may I say, exceptional cross-examination of the complainant," the judge said.

" The whole process was exactly as it should have been. "

In scenes that resembled a mock appeal, Mr Dann outlined 16 pieces of evidence the defence was challenging, pointing to alleged inconsistencies with the woman's account of the night in question and other events.

Ralph Carr appeared in the pre-sentence hearing without his trademark black wig. (ABC News)

Carr began crying in the court dock as Mr Dann described his mental health issues and history of suicide attempts.

Yesterday, he said Carr was in "a living hell" while in an isolated prison cell for 23 hours a day.

However, Mr Fisher, for the prosecution, said the court should be "circumspect" when considering evidence from Carr's psychiatrist about his mental health.

"There's a great deal of speculation about how things might eventuate if the accused man remains in custody for a significant period of time," he said.

Prosecutors are expected to address the judge further about the nature of Carr's offending and the impact on the victim tomorrow.

If the judge refuses Carr's stay application, he is likely to be sentenced next Thursday.

He could spend months in jail before the case is brought before Victoria's Court of Appeal.

World.title: What you need to know about the working holiday visa pause
World.content:
The federal government has paused visa applications for working holiday-makers from 24 countries.

The temporary visa provides access to young people from overseas to fill labour shortages while travelling in Australia.

Here is what we know about the pause and countries affected, as experts weigh-in on the impact on industries that rely on these visa holders.

What is a working holiday-maker visa?

It is still unclear why working holiday visa applications have been paused from the two dozen countries. (Flickr: Slim Teller)

The Working Holiday Maker (WHM) program started in 1975 and was launched to promote cultural exchange between young people from Australia and around the world.

It started with an uncapped visa stream known as the 417 subclass, which now has 19 partner countries including Canada, France, Japan and the United Kingdom.

Decades later a separate capped WHM visa stream, known as subclass 462, began and now includes 29 countries.

Indonesia, China and the US were the top three citizenship countries of subclass 462 visas in the six-month period to June 30, last year, according to the Department of Home Affairs.

As of June 30, 2025 there were 206,187 working holiday-makers in Australia.

What does a 'pause' mean?

At a press conference in Sydney on Sunday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the WHM visas were "being processed more slowly than they were previously".

He did not comment further on the changes.

On the website for the Work and Holiday visa subclass 462, applications for visas from 24 countries have been paused.

The website says applications are temporarily paused when the cap is nearly filled or to spread out visa applications lodgements throughout the program year.

"Lodgements may also be paused to support the Government's migration settings while ensuring the program operates sustainably," the page reads.

Tony Burke says the WHM visas were "being processed more slowly than they were previously". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Immigration lawyer Chris Johnston, who has worked in the industry for decades, said the government's actions were "dramatic".

"I do believe [in the past], they have paused, or run out of allocations, so these sort of things have happened before," Mr Johnston told ABC.

" But when you look at the screen, [almost] the whole screen is blue [paused]. So this is different to one country running out of allocations, or a one-off pause. "

Applications from 24 countries have been paused according to the Department of Home Affairs website. (Department of Home Affairs)

He also said the changes were not officially announced.

"It was just something that was put up on the website of the Department of Home Affairs," he said.

"It was quietly put out there."

Which countries are affected?

Applications from almost all of the 29 countries that are part of the capped working holiday-maker visa stream have been paused.

It includes countries with higher caps, such as Indonesia, Spain, Argentina and Singapore.

Indonesia, which has an annual allocation of 5,000 places for working holiday-maker applicants, is among the countries subject to the pause. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

Applications are still being accepted from five countries.

San Marino and Türkiye have 100 places each — on a first in, first served basis — while China, India and Vietnam operate on a ballot system.

Countries facing WHV application pause Argentina

Austria

Brazil

Chile

Czech Republic

Ecuador

Greece

Hungary

Indonesia

Israel

Luxembourg

Malaysia

Mongolia

Papua New Guinea

Peru

Poland

Portugal

Singapore

Slovak Republic

Slovenia

Spain

Switzerland

Thailand

Uruguay Source: Department of Home Affairs

Why are the visa applications paused?

It is still unclear why applications have been paused, but experts say it might have to do with a broader discussion about net overseas migration, or NOM.

"Many visa programs are suffering, either through slow processing, there's a high number of refusals for student visas, and now we can see that attention is also being turned to working holiday visas," Mr Johnston said.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, NOM is the number of incoming migrant arrivals minus outgoing migrant departures over a specific period.

The Labor government aims to cut net migration to 225,000 people annually. (AAP: Bianca de Marchi)

If the government's objective was to reduce net overseas migration, Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration, said "slow processing is a very, very poor way to do it".

"Slow processing usually just creates more problems than it solves," he said.

"It's a short-term solution to a long-term problem."

WHV holders have the option to extend their visas for up to three years and Mr Rizvi said removing the final year, that was introduced during the COVID pandemic, would be a "sensible" move from a net migration perspective.

In a statement to the ABC, the Department of Home Affairs did not specifically address the pause.

"Reforms to the Working Holiday Maker (WHM) program will better control demand and provide a fairer allocation of WHM visas," a department spokesperson said.

How does this impact visa applicants?

Wendi Aylward, a spokesperson for the Backpacker and Youth Tourism panel (BYTAP), said the industry received "very little information" from the government.

"Those who had applied under the 417 or 462 visa after July 1, anyone who's contacted Immigration to try and get an update on their visa have just been told that they need to wait," she said.

"And remember we're now in mid-August, so we have people that applied in early July and are still waiting."

Wendi Aylward from the Backpacker and Youth Tourism panel says the organisation has received minimal information on the visa pause. (Supplied)

Mr Johnston said the pause would be a "big problem" for applicants who had not lodged their application.

"The pause basically means they will not be able to lodge a new one whilst it's paused … so they will have to change their plans and wait until it opens again," he said.

"But when it opens, it might not be as easy to get as it previously was."

Mr Rizvi said the slowdown would be "quite unfair" for applicants.

"A pause or a slowdown just means the backlog of applications builds up," he said.

"All those applicants would be legally valid applications and would have to be processed, so you haven't actually solved any problem."

How does it impact Australia?

Ms Aylward said working holiday-maker visa holders play an "important" role in regional Australia, especially in the horticulture industry.

"Those farmers [in regional areas] may need someone only for a week or a couple of days, and that's where a working holiday-maker becomes just so critical," she said.

"They are regionally dispersed, and the wonderful thing is they spend the money that they make in those communities."

Mr Burke said the Pacific Workers Scheme was the "principal visa for the agricultural industry". (Supplied: Backpacker and Youth Tourism Panel)

In 2019, working holiday-makers contributed $3.2 billion to the Australian economy, according to Tourism Australia.

The tourism body reported at least $726 million of that was spent in regional areas.

Ms Aylward said there was concern about what the pause would mean for the tourism sector.

"Working holiday-makers create jobs in regional Australia because they use the travel operators, they go to the bakeries, they stay at the hostels," she said.

"So, they not only do the work themselves, but they facilitate and create employment in Australia."

NSW modern slavery report NSW parliamentary inquiry finds evidence of migrant workers living in near uninhabitable conditions, forced to work demanding hours and threatened if they spoke up.

When questioned on the impact of the visa processing for the agricultural industry, Mr Burke said the Pacific Workers Scheme or PALM was the "principal visa for the agricultural industry".

Mr Rizvi said that answer surprised him given the "massive levels of exploitation and abuse" that were detailed in a report on that scheme from a NSW parliamentary inquiry.

"I'm surprised the government is encouraging people to apply for the Pacific visa that has so many different problems," he said.

World.title: Breaking: WA Police appeal for help to find missing 10-year-old girl
World.content:
Western Australian police are searching for a 10-year-old girl who has been missing from Perth for three days.

Lyndel Ningella was last seen in the northern suburb of Butler around 6pm on Saturday, August 15.

It is believed she was wearing a black jumper and black shorts and may have travelled to the suburbs of Kwinana, Leda, Parmelia or Wellard.

Assistant Superintendent Darren Hart said police were concerned for her safety.

"We hold concerns for Lyndel due to her young age and believe she may be staying with family and associates," he told reporters.

Assistant Superintendent Darren Hart said police were concerned for her safety. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

"It's believed she may have travelled to the Wellard area, in the Mandurah police district and was possibly there across the weekend.

"We are concerned for her safety in that she is a 10-year-old girl who is making her own way in the world."

Lyndel is described as being about 160 centimetres tall with a medium build, brown eyes and long brown hair with blonde ends.

Anyone who sees Lyndel or has information on her whereabouts is urged to contact police immediately.

World.title: Family of missing 18yo hiker confronts 'unimaginable situation'
World.content:
The family of missing bushwalker Lily Hooper is dealing with an "unimaginable situation" as the search for the 18-year-old continues.

Ms Hooper left her home south-west of Sydney last Wednesday morning to go hiking in the Nattai National Park in the Southern Highlands.

Her car was later found near the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail, but despite an extensive multi-agency operation beginning on Wednesday night, there has been no trace of the experienced bushwalker.

Efforts to find Lily Hooper have continued on day seven. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

'Beloved daughter'

The family released a statement through NSW Police today.

"Our family is absolutely devastated that our beloved daughter Lily is missing," the family said.

"We would like to thank all the emergency services and volunteers for their support and continued commitment to the search, not only during the day but throughout the night."

They wrote that they were "desperate" to bring Lily home safe and asked the community to keep the family and Lily in their thoughts.

"We appreciate people who have made offers for the search, but due to the terrain and conditions we ask just professional search teams continue," the family wrote in the statement.

" We also ask for privacy and understanding as our family navigates this unimaginable situation. "

Search continues

The search is now in its seventh day today, but authorities said they had not given up hope of finding the experienced bushwalker.

Search teams from multiple agencies were on the ground today. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Specialist police crews were joined by 200 teams from the SES and rescue helicopters at the command site today, where they have been taking turns to work through the trail day and night.

Crews scoured dense bush, deep ravines and clifftops in their search and have battled inclement weather, which is expected to clear on Thursday.

NSW Police said there had been no trace of Ms Hooper or her belongings, and that her family was assisting in the search effort.

Search teams have battled extremely difficult terrain during the search. (Supplied: VRA NSW)

The terrain has been described as "incredibly rough", vast and dense, complicating efforts to cover the search area.

Police previously said they were unable to determine Ms Hooper's intended route beyond the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail, and whether she reached a nearby peak.

They previously said they believed Ms Hooper had her mobile phone with her and they were continuing to examine telecommunications information that could help establish where she went after arriving at the national park.

World.title: Photos of bedside rifle cartridges shown to Bogie triple murder trial
World.content:
The trial of a Queensland cattle farmer, accused of murdering the owners of a neighbouring property, has viewed photos of rifle cartridge packets found inside his home.

Prosecutors have told a Supreme Court trial being held in Townsville that spent shell casings with "30.30 WIN RP" markings were found around the bodies of married couple Mervyn Schwarz and Maree Schwarz and Mrs Schwarz's son Graham Tighe.

Maree Schwarz (left), Mervyn Schwarz and Graham Tighe (right) were found dead outside the gate of a Bogie cattle station in 2022. (Supplied/ABC News)

The jury heard the trio were found fatally wounded outside the gate of Darryl Valroy Young's Bogie cattle station on August 4, 2022.

Mr Young, who was charged over their deaths, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder.

He has also pleaded not guilty to the attempted murder of Ross Tighe, who earlier told the trial he was shot by Mr Young, and saw the farmer shoot dead his family.

Photographs taken by police investigators and presented to the trial today showed two packets of cartridges for a .30-30 calibre rifle.

The court heard the packets were found inside Mr Young's home, beside medication prescribed to him, next to a bed.

Monique Sheppard tendered photos of .30-30 rifle cartridges today. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Crown prosecutor Monique Sheppard presented the photos taken by Queensland Police Senior Constable Kerrod Vaughn and noted the absence of cartridges inside one of the packets.

"There seems to be five cartridges absent.

"That is correct," Senior Constable Vaughn replied.

The trial has heard that Mr Young was not licensed to carry a .30-30 calibre rifle and that no such weapon was found on his property, Shannonvale Station.

Mr Young's neighbour, Brett Stagg, earlier told the trial that he once owned a .30-30 calibre rifle but that it went missing during a fire at his property in 2011.

Darryl Young has taken notes throughout the trial. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Disconnected cameras

The trial has also viewed photos of trail cameras and dozens of memory cards inside Mr Young's kitchen, after Ross Tighe said cameras usually at the gate of Shannonvale Station were missing on the day of the alleged murders.

Ross Tighe was the first witness the crown called to give evidence in the trial of Darryl Valroy Young. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Photos of the bloodstained Land Cruiser driver's seat, where Mrs Schwarz was found dead, were also presented to the jury today.

Ms Sheppard tendered several photos of a small circular hole that could be seen in the damaged window of the driver-side door.

Photos of shell casings around the bodies of Mr Schwarz and Graham Tighe, who lay outside the Land Cruiser, were also presented to the jury yesterday.

Stepmother refused statement

The trial heard Mr Young was arrested late on August 4, 2022 alongside his son, Derek Young, and his stepmother, Sharon Young, as well as two wind-farm workers, but that only Mr Young was accused of wrongdoing.

His lawyer, Anthony J Kimmins, told the trial Mr Young never saw the Schwarzes or the Tighes on the day he is accused of shooting them.

Police revealed yesterday that Sharon Young refused repeated requests from detectives to give a statement in the days after the alleged shooting.

The trial has heard that Derek Young, who gave evidence last week, did provide police with a statement.

Derek Young told the trial he saw his father talking to Sharon Young after Darryl Young had returned from the station gate on the morning of August 4, 2022.

He said his father and Sharon Young also travelled together in an all-terrain vehicle later that day to meet with wind-farm workers installing equipment at the property.

The trial continues.

World.title: 'Can't hide behind borders': Police arrest hundreds of DV offenders during blitz
World.content:
Fifteen men have been arrested in the ACT, and hundreds more in New South Wales, as part of cross-border family and domestic violence police operations.

ACT police's Operation Shepherd ran over five days last week to coincide with NSW Police's Operation Amarok, targeting family violence offenders.

ACT Policing Detective Superintendent Kylie Lawson said three people wanted by NSW Police were found living in Canberra, while one man was arrested in NSW and extradited to the territory.

"Working together, we were able to locate these men and arrest them," she said.

ACT Policing's Operation Shepherd ran over five days last week to coincide with NSW Police's Operation Amarok. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Police also seized two firearms, ammunition and drugs after arresting a 51-year-old man who was also served with a family violence order.

Another man was charged with multiple offences after allegedly assaulting his partner over several years.

On top of the 15 arrests, a further five men received summons to face the ACT Magistrates Court for family violence-related offences or breaches of orders and conditions.

ACT Policing seized two firearms, ammunition, and cannabis plants after arresting a 51-year-old man. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Detective Superintendent Lawson said steps had also been taken during the operation to improve police responses to family violence.

"In the ACT, we have updated offenders' vehicle registration details so if they're stopped by police, for whatever reason, we can see that they have conditions not to contact their victim and ensure that there is no one else in the vehicle who is not supposed to be there," she said.

" The community can be assured that there is zero tolerance for domestic and family violence in the ACT and New South Wales. "

Detective Superintendent Kylie Lawson and Superintendent Danielle Emerton have warned domestic violence offenders that police will find them. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Detective Superintendent Lawson said the operations were an opportunity to put family violence offenders on notice.

"We take family violence seriously every day of the year, but operations such as these allow us to pool our resources and information and target those people who have evaded police detection," she said.

Hundreds of arrests across NSW

Operation Amarok also saw 732 arrests made across New South Wales and 1,589 charges laid over three days.

Police also conducted 1,497 bail compliance checks and 12,054 apprehended domestic violence order compliance checks, with a total of 546 breaches identified.

More than 100 firearms and 16 weapons were also seized.

Some of the men arrested have been extradited across the border. (Supplied: NSW Police)

NSW Police has conducted Operation Amarok more than a dozen times, and Superintendent Danielle Emerton said NSW was pleased to share its "operational blueprint" with ACT Policing and work closely to extradite offenders.

"Operations like this have shown that we take domestic family violence very seriously and the safety of the community is paramount," she said.

She warned domestic violence offenders that they "can't run and can't hide".

"The New South Wales Police and ACT are working collaboratively. We share intelligence. We share resources, and we will find you," she said.

" There is no escaping. If you're a DV offender, then look out. "

NSW Police made hundreds of arrests across the state during Operation Amarok. (Supplied: NSW Police)

'Can't hide behind borders'

ACT Police Minister Marisa Paterson said she expected more joint operations in the future, noting that police worked closely with their counterparts in other jurisdictions on a daily basis.

"I think it sends a really strong message to perpetrators of domestic and family violence that they can't hide behind borders," she said.

Marisa Paterson says domestic and family violence is a whole-of-community issue. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The ACT government is currently moving to strengthen domestic and family violence laws, with legislation to make coercive control a standalone offence before the Legislative Assembly. Coercive control is already a standalone offence in NSW.

Dr Paterson said Australia was having the "cultural reckoning" it needed to have.

"In this day and age, we have seen the public discourse around domestic family and sexual violence really develop in Australia," she said.

"This is a whole-of-community issue. This is a cultural issue. This is societal change that is required.

World.title: Commonwealth accuses chemical giant of hiding health impacts of PFAS
World.content:
A US chemical manufacturer stands accused of withholding evidence that its firefighting products used by the Australian Defence Force were toxic and did not break down in the environment.

A mammoth Federal Court claim brought by the Australian government against 3M labels the company's actions "intentional and reprehensible".

It claims that by 1979, 3M knew that variants of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contained in its firefighting foam "persist indefinitely, bioaccumulate and bio-concentrate in both humans and animals", were potentially toxic to animals and could migrate into drinking water.

The Commonwealth alleges that 3M and 3M Australia "continued to manufacture, market, distribute and sell" aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) for another 24 years, until at least 2003.

The statement of claim alleges "conscious, contumelious, contemptuous or outrageous disregard for the rights of the Commonwealth and the broader Australian public, including Defence personnel and those living in the areas surrounding the Bases, who have been affected by the presence and continued migration of … PFAS contamination".

During the first case management hearing on August 7, Justice Catherine Button described the 1,600-page document as "daunting", while 3M's counsel said it was the "most complex matter" they had ever seen.

Chemicals contained in firefighting foam used at the Williamtown RAAF base are now at the centre of a water contamination scare. (CRC CARE)

In its largest ever legal claim, the government announced in May it was seeking $2 billion in damages arising from PFAS contamination at 28 Defence bases across Australia and the areas surrounding them.

Large quantities of the foam were discharged in and around each of the sites during training and operational activities over about 30 years.

The ABC has obtained the statement of claim in which the Commonwealth alleges the use of 3M's AFFF "resulted in significant contamination" of land and water, including drinking water, that posed risks to human and animal health and the environment.

The Commonwealth said it had incurred "substantial costs", including $214 million for undertaking investigations, remediation and ongoing monitoring, and $367 million in settlements from five class actions brought against the government.

The damages sought are also designed to cover future costs the Commonwealth expects to incur, including further claims alleging loss and damage.

The federal government has faced multiple class actions from communities impacted by defence base contamination. (Four Corners)

The 28 bases have been split into three categories for the case.

The highest risk areas are those where PFAS is continuing to leach, new areas are being contaminated and guideline values for acceptable PFAS levels in drinking water or recreational waters are exceeded.

Seventeen bases fall under that definition, including Jervis Bay, Richmond and Wagga Wagga in NSW, Oakey and Townsville in Queensland, Darwin and Tindal in the Northern Territory and Williams and Bandiana in Victoria.

AFFF's history in Australia

The claim lays out the history of AFFF, which dates back to 1962 when 3M, at the request of the United States Navy, began developing alternative options for firefighting foams that could be used to extinguish petroleum fires.

In 1972, several years after members of the Australian Defence Force attended 3M product demonstrations, the Commonwealth began purchasing AFFF.

It met the requirements of the US Military and was marketed as "the most effective foaming agent ever developed", the court documents state.

The government points to various statements made by 3M or 3M Australia from 1973 which claimed the product was "non-toxic to humans … was biodegradable and was not expected to adversely affect the ecology of receiving streams in the vicinity of its use".

The federal government said it continued to purchase the product until 2003 on the condition that it did not have any significant detrimental effect on the environment or present a waste disposal problem.

3M Company has manufactured PFAS chemicals since the 1950s. (Supplied: 3M)

Internal reports detail risks

The Commonwealth's lawyers say 3M falsely made those assurances, citing 310 internal company documents including testing reports and environmental data sheets.

The claim cites a toxicity study conducted by 3M in 1978 which found rhesus monkeys died within the first few days of exposure to a component in AFFF until concentrations were significantly lowered, and even at lower doses the animals exhibited signs of toxicity, including gastrointestinal distress.

The government also refers to a document prepared in 1998 that identified PFOS, a type of PFAS, had been found in the blood of rats not knowingly exposed to it, concluding that " there was a significant risk of ecological harm due to environmental levels of PFOS".

The author of that report resigned from 3M in 1999, citing concerns about the dangers of PFOS and "profound disappointment" in 3M's handling of environmental risks associated with the manufacture and use of PFOS and its precursors, the documents state.

In 1981, 3M implemented and publicly announced a policy of not permitting women "of child bearing potential" to work at its Decatur, Alabama plant, "so they will not be exposed to a type of fluorochemical that can cause birth defects in rats".

The Commonwealth referred to another 3M document titled Project Spring Communication Plan dated May 2000 when it announced it would phase out certain products containing PFAS, including some firefighting foams.

The STOP PFAS group has identified firefighting foam used at a petrol tanker crash in 1992 as the main source of contamination. (Supplied)

It stated, "very small amounts of materials from this chemistry are widespread in the environment, including humans, and are persistent" but "existing scientific evidence indicates that the presence of these materials at extremely low levels does not pose a human health or environmental risk".

"This is like a small piece of plastic by the side of the road … it doesn't do any harm, but you'd rather not see it there," the internal document read.

The Commonwealth alleges "despite holding information about the properties and risks associated with these variants of PFAS, 3M took … no meaningful steps to properly or adequately warn purchasers of 3M AFFF as to those risks, or of appropriate measures that ought to have been taken to contain or minimise the release of PFAS into the broader environment".

The ABC has contacted 3M for comment.

When Attorney-General Michelle Rowland announced the legal action in May, a 3M spokesperson said in a statement that the company would "defend ourselves against these claims through the legal process".

"3M has never manufactured PFAS in Australia and ceased sales of the products at issue in Australia around two decades ago," the statement said.

"Despite this, the Department of Defence continued to use PFAS-containing firefighting foams for nearly two decades longer."

The matter will return to court on October 16.

World.title: Veterans gather to mark 60 years since the Battle of Long Tan
World.content:
Vietnam War veteran Graeme Davis struggles to find the words to talk about what he went through during the conflict.

"It's almost impossible to describe unless you have been in battle," Mr Davis said.

"Unless you've actually looked down the barrel of a weapon ... and having to make a moral and ethical decision whether to pull the trigger."

Graeme Davis, of the 26 Australians of the 6th Battalion in The Royal Australian Regiment (6RAR), was wounded in the Battle of Long Tan. (Supplied: William James Cunneen, Australian War Memorial)

Mr Davis said despite Australia's ultimate victory at the Battle of Long Tan, it was overall a long conflict that saw the Australians mostly overpowered by their enemy.

And there was a moment on the afternoon of August 18 when he believed they would not survive at Long Tan either.

"Virtually we had less than probably 60 rounds of ammunition between us, we had less than 60 soldiers still alive or wounded, that were able to continue to protect and fight the battle," he said.

" And we virtually thought 'within the next 60 minutes, it will be all over for us, we won't be here'. "

He said it was in that moment that the "reality" of the war came home to him.

"That we were totally outnumbered ... we never had the resources or the people to defend ourselves, or even at that stage do a tactical withdrawal," he said.

A significant day

Fought in a rubber plantation called Long Tan, the battle was one of the most significant engagements involving Australians during the war.

The first Australian soldiers of the Royal Australian Regiment's D Company had arrived in south Vietnam in May of 1966, and within two months, some of them were at Long Tan.

The villagers of Long Tan and Long Phuoc had been relocated by the Australians to secure a new base, prompting Vietnamese troops to attack in a bid to recover them.

Australian troops, alongside soldiers from New Zealand and the United States, were victorious at Long Tan. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

The Australians were joined by New Zealand's 161 Field Battery and soldiers from the US in what would become a victory over the Vietnamese.

As a result of the battle, 18 Australians were killed and 24 wounded.

By the time it was over on the evening of August 18, the North Vietnamese suffered hundreds of casualties.

Remembering the fallen

Uniformed military personnel lay wreaths at the ceremony in Canberra. (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

Today, 60 years on, veterans and their families laid wreaths to honour those who died in the conflict at the Australian Vietnam Forces National Memorial in Canberra.

Governor-General Samantha Mostyn, Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh and Australian War Memorial director Matt Anderson were among those who attended the ceremony.

The anniversary coincides with Vietnam Veterans' Day, something that is meaningful for many who fought in the conflict.

ACT Vietnam Veterans Federation president Ward Gainey said the ceremony was a chance to commemorate those who served in the war, and their families.

"We take this opportunity to remember, to understand the families who are involved, those who returned and are still trying to live with their memories and making sure we support them as they grow older," he said.

ACT Vietnam Veterans Federation Ward Gainey at the commemoration of the Battle of Long Tan. (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

Mr Gainey said the day was a reminder that serving in the defence force was not just "putting on your suit and going to work".

"It's important, I think, that we don't forget what people do," he said.

"These are hardships … we go away, and we know that we're going to a place that is dangerous.

"But another time, during peacetime, we are still there to be a part of the nation that we love and the nation we have to protect, and we are honoured to do so."

Keeping the stories alive

Reverend Mick O'Donnell, who served in the navy in Vietnam, read the prayer for peace at the memorial.

He said it was vital veterans' stories continued to be told.

"I think of the collegiality, getting together with the colleagues and remembering stories and remembering the days when we were all together and doing various things, but also just to recognise that we're getting older," he said.

" It's good to keep the memory alive, I think. I love the stories. "

Veteran Mick O'Donnell said he hoped those in power would think of "love instead of war". (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

Reverend O'Donnell said he hoped the leaders present remembered the importance of peace and love, as conflicts continue around the world.

"They are in the position where they are making decisions for our involvement in conflicts in the future," he said.

" I hope today that ... they might stop and think about love instead of war. "

'Never been fully accepted'

Graeme Davis with a Red Cross nurse in a military hospital in 1966. (Supplied: Graeme Davis)

To this day, some of those who served in Vietnam still feel the sting of what they perceived as the Australian public ignoring or not recognising their sacrifice and service.

"It was something outside our control and the public were demonstrating against the government of the day and the action of the day, and taking it out on the veterans rather than saying, 'You weren't responsible, you were doing what your nation asked you to do'," Mr Davis said.

He said the Battle of Long Tan was equal to any other major military engagement in Australia's wartime history.

"I think anyone who has studied military history or read military history, you would have been familiar that there's probably been more accounts of Long Tan written equal to the landing at Gallipoli," he said.

World.title: BHP reports 113 sexual harassment cases in 12 months
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWorkplace safety BHP reports 113 sexual harassment cases in 12 months Simon Johanson Updated August 18, 2026 — 5:39pm ,first published August 18, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Almost 150 BHP employees were subjected to sexual harassment, including indecent touching and stalking, or racial abuse in just 12 months, leading to 131 sackings and resignations at the mining giant in response. BHP’s ethics and investigation unit handled 113 complaints of harassment in the 12 months to July, which were detailed in the company’s annual report released on Tuesday, and more than two dozen cases of racial abuse. At least 125 cases weren’t investigated because of insufficient information or the wishes of the impacted person. BHP has disclosed more than 100 staff were sexually harassed or racially abused. Bloomberg The mining industry, which often accommodates large groups of mostly male workers in remote camps, has suffered a wave of damaging sexual harassment claims in recent years. Both BHP and rival miner Rio Tinto were subject to separate class actions in 2024 alleging harassment and sex discrimination against female employees, which are still before the courts.



Rio Tinto commissioned an independent report that found in 2022 sexual harassment was widespread among its fly-in, fly-out workers. A parliamentary inquiry uncovered similar allegations at BHP in 2021. Another mining giant, Fortescue, is also facing a class-action lawsuit from female employees who allege widespread sexual harassment and assault, including reports of men stealing their underwear from public laundries and being unable to go to the gym because men touched them inappropriately. Overall, BHP said the number of reported cases fell from the previous year and none involved “sexual assault”. However, a large proportion involved sexualised and indecent touching and other cases included sexually aggressive comments, stalking, image-based harassment and jokes or sexualised conversations, the company said. “People who may have been impacted by sexual harassment or racial harassment are offered specialised support … The response is guided by the impacted person’s preferences and the nature and severity of the alleged misconduct,” BHP said. On the commercial front, the world’s biggest miner said it will pay its Australian shareholders a $12 billion dividend bonanza, as copper prices hit records amid soaring global demand for green energy, electric vehicles and AI data centres.



BHP shrugged off heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and rising diesel prices to declare a final dividend of US99¢ ($1.39) per share, taking its total payout for the year to $US1.72 a share, up from $US1.10 the previous year. The global resources giant’s full-year $US8.7 billion ($12.2 billion) return is the biggest payout for its shareholders in four years. BHP has pivoted to copper as its future key commodity after China’s economic slowdown and fresh supply entering the market heralded the end of a decades-long iron ore boom, which had fuelled its profits in recent years. It’s now the world’s largest copper producer. Related Article Critical minerals Pentagon ploughs $560 million into ‘world-first’ Australian mining project The move is paying off for the miner, with the price of copper, a metal essential to conducting electricity, near record highs – around $US6.70 per pound (454 grams) – as global demand for green energy and AI-driven data banks rockets. Shortages of copper concentrates and other feedstocks in China are crimping output from its smelters, adding to price pressures. The red metal’s upward trajectory is also being underpinned by a slump in production from Chile’s state-owned miner, Codelco, a top producer. Copper traders, worried about US President Donald Trump slapping tariffs on copper, are also stockpiling the metal into US warehouses, pushing up demand.



And BHP is benefiting. Its shares rose 2.7 per cent, giving it a market value of $316 billion and cementing its place as the biggest company on the ASX. Releasing its latest full-year results on Tuesday morning, the mining giant said its net profit rose 9 per cent to $US9.8 billion, as revenues jumped 15 per cent to $US58.8 billion. More than half of those profits are now derived from its copper mines in Australia, Chile and Argentina. “Copper is the engine that is driving BHP’s growth,” newly appointed chief executive Brandon Craig said. “For the first time, copper contributed more than half our underlying [earnings] and generated significant free cash flow, which means our copper growth is self-funding.” The miner maintains a well-defined project pipeline of copper assets that it said can potentially lift its copper production up to 40 per cent by 2035. BHP said it had managed to decrease costs across its operations by 6.1 per cent despite headwinds from inflation, higher diesel prices and global supply chain disruptions.



At the same time, Chinese demand for iron ore, a key ingredient of steelmaking, still remains resilient, it said. BHP’s iron ore mines in Australia’s remote Pilbara region produced a record 265 million tonnes of ore, generating about $US14 billion in underlying earnings for the company. What BHP calls its “byproducts” – the gold, uranium and silver that are often found alongside copper – added $US4.5 billion to its bottom line. World.title: ‘Let the public be the judge’: Coalition says PM, Wong and others must front royal commission
World.content:
The Coalition has called on the Albanese government to extend the deadline for the Bondi royal commission beyond the one-year anniversary, demanding that government ministers, muslim clerics and high-profile figures from the arts be called before the inquiry to account for rising antisemitism. As the commission’s final day of hearings approaches, Liberal MP Julian Leeser told parliament on Tuesday that the commission had been unable to do its job properly without government ministers appearing, such as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, the attorney-general and the ministers for education, home affairs and foreign affairs. Liberal MP Julian Leeser speaks in the House of Representatives on Tuesday. Dominic Lorrimer He also said there were more questions to ask of leaders of arts institutions, universities, protest movements and the human rights commission – some of whom have already appeared – as well as people such as former Coalition treasurer Josh Frydenberg, who was told he would not be called. “This week is the final sitting week of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion,” Leeser said during a suspension of standing orders early Tuesday afternoon.



“The royal commission is, for many Australians, the only chance we will have as a nation to properly expose and address the antisemitism that has become so prevalent in this country and which diminishes us all. Related Article Exclusive

Extremism Former Taliban extremist warns social division will only inspire more terror attacks “But it is a royal commission that finishes in a matter of days, and as it stands, it is a royal commission with unfinished business. The window to debate the issue is closing.” Leeser, a Jewish MP from north-west Sydney, has repeatedly condemned the Albanese government over its handling of antisemitism in the community since the Hamas attacks spurred Israel’s war on Gaza in 2023. The Executive Council of Australian Jewry declined to comment on whether the royal commission should be extended.



A senior figure in the Jewish community, speaking on condition of anonymity, said community leaders were “not clamouring” for the royal commission’s reporting date to be pushed back because they feared the inquiry could lose momentum and public support. Naveed Akram and his father, Sajid, are accused of carrying out the Bondi Beach attack that claimed 15 innocent lives, after being radicalised by IS propaganda. The Albanese government announced the royal commission into the Bondi tragedy and antisemitism after considerable political and social pressure in the weeks after the attack on December 14 last year. Commissioner Virginia Bell was tasked with delivering a final report by December 14 this year. From the day it was announced, the reporting date was seen as a tight deadline, but Bell has insisted she is determined to meet it. The commission has held nine blocks of hearings since May, covering the nature of antisemitism, universities and their encampments, as well as a range of public services. Other sessions focused on the terrorism threat level and security arrangements at the Bondi event, law enforcement co-ordination, and the safety of the Jewish community. The commission has heard from Jewish Australians as well as ASIO director-general Mike Burgess, law enforcement, counter-terrorism experts, some high-level public servants, several university vice-chancellors and students.



But Leeser said it had not gone far enough. He named several people in the arts and cultural sector who should appear, including writers Clementine Ford and John Menadue, as well as the heads of Creative Australia. He said former vice-chancellors Genevieve Bell from ANU and Duncan Maskell from the University of Melbourne should appear. He also told parliament that Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi and NSW state MP Jenny Leong, who have attended pro-Palestine protests, should be called, as should Sydney protest leader Josh Lees and Islamic preacher Wissam Haddad. He said that the human rights commission, which has appeared, had “not been asked in any serious way to account for their failure to stand up for Australian Jews”. Finally, Leeser said Albanese, Tony Burke, Jason Clare, Michelle Rowland and Penny Wong should “show the courage and commitment to front the royal commission and be accountable”. “Answer questions. Explain your decisions and actions in the two years leading up to Bondi. Let the commission and the public be the judge,” he said. Coalition shadow treasurer Tim Wilson spoke in support of Leeser.



Labor did not support the debate being had in the House of Representatives, but Burke spoke afterwards to say he respected both Leeser and Wilson’s arguments. Related Article Crime The new brand of hate radicalising Australian teens He said the division over having the debate did not signal any division within the parliament about the horror of antisemitism. “I wanted to pay respect to both members who’ve spoken, and to respect absolutely that while there are differences in terms of whether the royal commission should be extended or whether it should keep to its initial timeline, there is no division within this parliament about the horrific nature of antisemitism,” he said. Burke said the horrors of the Bondi attack and antisemitism in Australia both before and since that moment were “unilaterally rejected by every member of this house”.



“While there is a difference in the process, I don’t want to offer anything other than respect to the members for the arguments that they’ve just put,” he said. World.title: David Gonski’s plan to end hate starts with ethics lessons for all students
World.content:
PoliticsNSWAntisemitism royal commission David Gonski’s plan to end hate starts with ethics lessons for all students Alexandra Smith August 18, 2026 — 5:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Businessman and former university chancellor David Gonski wants ethics classes similar to those in NSW public schools to be rolled out across all levels of education, and lessons in antisemitism to start as early as preschool, in a bid to combat hate in Australia. Gonski, the author of two seminal reports into school funding for the Gillard and Turnbull governments and chair of the federal antisemitism education taskforce, told the royal commission on antisemitism on Tuesday that education was key to improving social cohesion. Veteran businessman David Gonski (left) at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. Brent Lewin The veteran board director and former UNSW chancellor said his taskforce – which had met monthly since being appointed by the federal government days after the December 14 Bondi massacre – had been presented with several initiatives which he said showed significant merit. He singled out NSW Education Department boss Murat Dizdar’s decision to devote one of his annual staff development days to social cohesion, a move Gonski said was a mark of strong leadership.



Related Article Antisemitism royal commission ‘Let the public be the judge’: Coalition says PM, Wong and others must front royal commission Gonski also said it was his “passion”, supported by the taskforce, to see ethics classes offered across all levels of education. He said the business sector could also benefit from such teachings. “There is a thing called Primary Ethics and amazing as it may sound, Primary Ethics is only taught in NSW to those who don’t go to religious classes, which, if you think about it, is a bit odd,” Gonski told the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. “I think that the concept of having an ethics institute around Australia, which is available to run primary, secondary, and as I mentioned, tertiary, should be something that’s very important going forwards.” Primary Ethics is the sole-approved provider of ethics in more than 500 NSW public primary schools and was introduced in 2011 as a secular alternative to scripture classes.



“And I should also add, because nobody’s beyond reproach, maybe there should also be ethics for business, and so on as an extra adjunct, to actually ask questions like: what is the right thing to do? Just as Socrates asked. We think that’s quite a compelling [idea],” Gonski said. David Gonski told the royal commission he wanted lessons in antisemitism to start as early as preschool. Gonksi said the taskforce believed education on social cohesion should start as early as preschool. He was also hopeful the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority review of the school curriculum would lead to not only more education about the Holocaust but also the contributions of Jews and the Jewish faith to Australia. Counsel assisting Richard Lancaster asked him about Education Minister Jason Clare’s initiative to require universities to adopt a definition of antisemitism. Gonski hoped the new rules would “state one or two definitions acceptable under the standard”, but not be so open-ended as to allow universities to pick any definition they like. Gonski said he accepted that “many” prefer the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition, but he thought it would be a “very good solution” to allow universities to choose between that or the Universities Australia definition.



Related Article Exclusive

Extremism Former Taliban extremist warns social division will only inspire more terror attacks As chair of the government’s antisemitism education taskforce, Gonski was given 12 months to bring together state education ministries, universities, tertiary education authorities, private and religious schools, and the Australian Children’s Education & Care Quality Authority, the agency with oversight of the pre-school sector, to develop a response. Jillian Segal, Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, is also a member of the taskforce. World.title: Sydney council pulls book critical of Israel from library shelves
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature Sydney council pulls book critical of Israel from library shelves Melanie Kembrey August 18, 2026 — 5:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney council has pulled a book scrutinising Israel’s actions in Gaza from its library shelves pending a “review”. Waverley Council confirmed How to Sell a Genocide: The Media’s Complicity in the Destruction of Gaza, by US writer Adam Johnson, had been withdrawn from Waverley Library. The library serves Bondi and surrounding suburbs in Sydney’s east, home to one of Australia’s largest Jewish communities and close to the site of the December 2025 massacre. The book was seen at Waverley Library. . “Like most public libraries, Waverley Council outsources its book curation, ordering and purchasing, meaning book selection is not undertaken by council officers,” a council spokesperson said on Tuesday. “The book has been removed from library shelves for review, and council will further consider processes to ensure closer oversight of book selection.” The move follows a report by Jewish news service JWire last week that a survivor of the Bondi Beach massacre had posted on Facebook that she was distressed to see the book displayed on the new-release “What’s Hot” shelf of Waverley Library.



Adam H. Johnson’s book How to Sell a Genocide The Media’s Complicity in the Destruction of Gaza was removed by Waverley Library. The council received multiple complaints about the book, which remains listed in the library’s catalogue and is still available to reserve. The book was published in April by Pluto Press, a long-established British publisher that describes itself as a “radical political publishing house”. The book argues that Israel’s war in Gaza could not have continued without the “active, sustained complicity” of US media, and that major news outlets “systematically sanitised Israel’s war crimes, hid the US’s central role, and dehumanised the Palestinian people”. Pluto Press and Johnson have been contacted for comment. “They seem to be objecting largely based on the title using the word ‘genocide’,” Johnson was quoted in The Guardian as saying. “But ‘genocide’ is not my word, or my finding. The fact of genocide in Gaza is the overwhelming consensus of the human rights world, and it is a wholly mainstream opinion among those tasked with studying and determining such matters.



“That it makes some people upset is unfortunate, but reality is often upsetting. This particular reality is especially upsetting … to the parents of the over 20,000 children killed by Israel in Gaza since October 2023. Do Sydney officials plan on removing pro-Israel books from their libraries because it potentially upsets these community members?” Waverley Council declined to answer questions about how many complaints it had received, its process for handling them, the criteria for removing books from its collection, when the review would be completed or whether its findings would be made public. Mayor Will Nemesh has been contacted for comment. The removal comes two months after the NSW parliament amended the Library Act to protect libraries’ freedom to collect material, with Arts Minister John Graham saying the changes would guard against a US-style wave of book bans and culture wars. There have been more than 300 attempts to exclude more than 180 titles from library shelves around Australia since 2023, according to reports to the Australian Library and Information Association (ALIA). In 2024, Cumberland City Council in Sydney’s west sparked national controversy by banning a children’s book about same-sex parents from its libraries – a decision councillors later overturned after protests and a fiery four-hour meeting.



“Selection and availability of items in a collection is made by library staff with professional expertise and experience and is not based on personal, cultural, political, moral, philosophical and/or religious views,” ALIA chief executive Cathie Warburton said. While public libraries have collection development policies governing what they stock, some – as appears the case with Waverley Council – outsource selection and purchasing of books to specialist suppliers that deal directly with publishers. Alex Ryvchin, co-chief executive officer of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, welcomed the book’s removal, saying it had “no place on the shelves of this library”. “A book of this sort has no place on the shelves of a library, especially one within minutes of where Australians were slaughtered in large part due to the dehumanisation of Jews precisely through this sort of libel,” Ryvchin said. “I commend the individual who spotted the book, herself a survivor of the massacre, and acted to have it removed.” The City of Sydney, Northern Beaches, City of Parramatta and Sutherland Shire are among the library networks that have Johnson’s book available to borrow.



Related Article Sydney councils Western Sydney council reverses controversial book ban after heated debate Waverley Greens councillor Ludovico Fabiano said the feelings of people distressed by the book needed to be taken into account, but defended the principle of allowing readers to make their own choice. “We live in a free society where we should be able to express ourselves, and sometimes that is uncomfortable,” Fabiano said. “I feel terrible for the person suffering at the moment – we all are suffering. But should it have been taken off the shelves or not? I’ll leave it up to the officers to work out. From a personal perspective, for me, it’s just another book that you find on the shelf, and you get the choice whether you want to read it or not.” What else is happening in the book world?
